incidents.title: One city melts one partition
incidents.brief: Ride events are keyed by city_id across 64 partitions. New Year's Eve in NYC sends 40% of 90k events/s to partition 17. Its consumer is at 98% CPU and 4.2M messages behind; 63 others idle.
incidents.constraint: Each driver's location updates must stay in order; cross-driver order does not matter.
incidents.question: Now, how should the topic be keyed so one city can't do this again?

choices.label: Key events by driver_id instead of city
choices.resultTitle: Load spreads, order holds
choices.resultBody: Millions of driver_ids hash evenly over 64 partitions, so NYC's 36k events/s lands on every consumer while each driver's updates still share one partition.

choices.label: Add 64 more consumers to the group
choices.resultTitle: Sixty-four new idle consumers
choices.resultBody: A partition is read by one consumer per group, so the new consumers sit idle and partition 17 still has a single reader at 98% CPU.

choices.label: Drop the key and spray events round-robin
choices.resultTitle: Drivers jump backwards on the map
choices.resultBody: Lag clears, but one driver's updates now land on different partitions and are consumed out of order; 2,900 stale positions overwrite fresh ones each second.

hints: Look at how the 90k events/s are spread across 64 partitions.
A consumer group gives each partition to exactly one consumer.
Pick a key with many values that still groups what must stay ordered.

mitigation.question: The live map is freezing across NYC right now. What stops the bleeding tonight?

choices.label: Drop p17's location pings older than 30 s, keep trip events

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Sheds data that is already superseded; buys time, not a fix.

choices.resultTitle: Map unfreezes, p17 still hot
choices.resultBody: A driver's position is replaced every 4 s, so the 4M stale pings are worthless to a live map. Skipping them while still processing trip events cuts p17's backlog from 4.2M to 400k in minutes. The partition is still hot; the key is still wrong.

choices.label: Move consumer p17 onto a pod with four times the cores
choices.resultTitle: Three new cores sit idle
choices.resultBody: The consumer loop handles partition 17 on one thread, so the extra cores do nothing. CPU on the busy core stays pinned and the backlog keeps growing past 4.5M.

choices.label: Restart the p17 consumer pod to clear its stuck state
choices.resultTitle: A rebalance pause on top of the backlog
choices.resultBody: Nothing was stuck: the restart triggers a rebalance that stops all 64 consumers for 40 s, and p17 resumes from its last commit with 4.8M messages waiting.

incidents.title: Forty consumers, twelve working
incidents.brief: An orders topic has 12 partitions and is 9M messages behind. The team scaled the consumer group from 12 to 40 pods, but lag keeps climbing at 3k/s.
incidents.constraint: Per-order ordering must hold; the topic is keyed by order_id and orders finish within minutes.
incidents.question: Why didn't scaling help, and what does?

choices.label: Grow the topic to 48 partitions for new orders
choices.resultTitle: Forty pods finally share work
choices.resultBody: With 48 partitions each of the 40 consumers owns one or two, so 9M messages drain in about 20 minutes; add them in a quiet window, since keys remap.

choices.label: Give each pod its own consumer group id to parallelize
choices.resultTitle: Every order processed forty times
choices.resultBody: Separate groups each read the whole topic, so all 40 pods process every order; the DB sees 40x writes and 4,100 duplicate errors a second.

choices.label: Double the consumer pod count again, from 40 to 80
choices.resultTitle: Sixty-eight pods now idle
choices.resultBody: Maximum group parallelism equals the partition count, so still only 12 pods get partitions and lag keeps growing at 3k/s.

hints: Count partitions, then count consumers doing real work.
A group can use at most one consumer per partition.
Raise the ceiling, not the headcount.

incidents.title: The group that never settles
incidents.brief: Analytics consumers poll 500 records and call an enrichment API per record. A batch now takes 6 minutes; max.poll.interval is 5. Pods get evicted, the group rebalances every 90 s, and lag hits 12M.
incidents.constraint: Enrichment calls average 700 ms and cannot get faster this week.
incidents.question: What stops the rebalance storm?

choices.label: Poll 50 records and use cooperative rebalancing
choices.resultTitle: Pods stop getting evicted
choices.resultBody: A 50-record batch finishes in about 35 s, well inside the 5-minute poll limit, and cooperative-sticky assignment moves only the partitions that change owner.

choices.label: Raise max.poll.interval.ms from 5 to 15 minutes
choices.resultTitle: Evictions stop; batches still take 6 minutes
choices.resultBody: With a 15-minute poll limit no pod is evicted, rebalances stop and lag starts draining, from 12M to 9M. Each poll still holds 500 records for 6 minutes, though, and batch time is creeping up as the enrichment API slows at peak.

choices.label: Scale the consumer group from 30 to 60 pods
choices.resultTitle: More members, longer rebalances
choices.resultBody: Only 30 partitions exist, and each extra member joining or leaving triggers another stop-the-world rebalance, so lag grows to 14M.

hints: Compare the batch time with max.poll.interval.
Evicted consumers trigger a rebalance for everyone.
Make each poll finish quickly and reshuffle less on rebalance.

culprit.explanation: The consumer logs show a 500-record batch taking 362 s against a 300 s max.poll.interval.ms, so each pod is kicked out mid-batch and the group rebalances. The enrichment API is slow but healthy.

wrongNodeFeedback.api: The API answers in about 700 ms with zero errors; it is slow by design this week. Look at what 500 of those calls in a row do to one poll.
wrongNodeFeedback.log: Brokers are healthy and producing steadily. The lag is a symptom of consumers that keep leaving the group.
wrongNodeFeedback.db: The warehouse is mostly idle, waiting for data. It is downstream of the problem.

log: produce rate steady at 15k msg/s, broker disk 41%
grp: consumer-12: processed batch of 500 records in 362 s
group analytics: rebalance #412, 30 members revoking partitions
api: enrich p50=690 ms p99=1.1 s, 0 errors
db: COPY clicks_enriched: 3k rows/s, no lock waits
loader idle 80% of the time waiting for batches

incidents.title: Ad clicks billed to the wrong minute
incidents.brief: A game counts ad clicks per minute by arrival time. Phones offline on the subway upload in bursts, so 09:00 shows a 6x spike and advertisers are billed 7% wrong per minute.
incidents.constraint: Billing is per minute of when the click happened; 99% of clicks arrive within 2 minutes.
incidents.question: How should the windows be defined?

choices.label: Window on event time with a 2-minute watermark
choices.resultTitle: Clicks land in the right minute
choices.resultBody: Each click counts in the minute it happened; the window closes once the watermark passes 2 minutes late, and the rare later clicks go to a correction feed.

choices.label: Keep arrival time but widen windows to one hour
choices.resultTitle: Still billed on arrival time
choices.resultBody: Hourly buckets hide the 09:00 spike, but a click made at 08:58 and uploaded at 09:03 still bills the wrong hour; per-minute billing is gone entirely.

choices.label: Discard clicks that arrive over 10 s late
choices.resultTitle: Real clicks thrown away
choices.resultBody: Subway uploads arrive minutes late, so about 9% of genuine clicks are dropped and advertisers are now underbilled instead of misbilled.

hints: When did the click happen versus when did it arrive?
Late data needs a rule for how long a window stays open.
Use the timestamp in the event, plus a lateness bound.

variants.constraint: Advertisers pay only for clicks that reach us within 10 seconds; offline taps can't be verified and are unbillable. Billing is per minute of arrival.

drop-late.resultBody: Clicks older than 10 s are unbillable by contract, so discarding them removes the subway bursts from 09:00. What remains arrived within 10 s, so arrival-minute counts match the invoice. The raw log still keeps dropped clicks for analytics.

event-time.resultBody: Event-time windows put every offline tap back in its minute, but those taps are unbillable. Invoices now include the subway bursts the contract excludes, and the 2-minute watermark delays every bill for nothing.

hints: Which clicks does the contract actually pay for?
A click that arrives late is not just misplaced here; it is unbillable.
If only fresh clicks count, arrival time is close enough to click time.

incidents.title: Wallet credited twice after a crash
incidents.brief: A wallet consumer writes credits to Postgres, then commits the Kafka offset. A pod OOM-killed between the two replays 2,000 events on restart; 0.3% of today's credits were paid twice.
incidents.constraint: Every credit event carries a unique event_id; money must be applied once.
incidents.question: How do you make credits effectively-once?

choices.label: Upsert by event_id, commit offsets in that transaction
choices.resultTitle: Replays become no-ops
choices.resultBody: A replayed event hits the unique event_id and does nothing, and storing the offset in the same Postgres transaction means credit and progress commit together.

choices.label: Commit the Kafka offset first, then write each credit
choices.resultTitle: Credits vanish instead
choices.resultBody: Committing first is at-most-once: a crash after the commit but before the write skips the event, so about 1,800 credits a day are never paid.

choices.label: Turn on Kafka transactions and idempotent producers
choices.resultTitle: Exactly-once stops at Kafka
choices.resultBody: Kafka transactions cover read-process-write between topics; the Postgres write sits outside them, so the crash still replays 2,000 credits.

hints: Which two writes can a crash separate?
Delivery is at least once; the sink must tolerate repeats.
Make the database the place that dedupes and remembers progress.

incidents.title: Three days of bad fraud scores
incidents.brief: A buggy fraud-model deploy wrote wrong risk scores for 72 hours. The transactions topic keeps 7 days (1.8B events). Live scoring must keep its 2 s freshness while you repair history.
incidents.constraint: The scores table is rebuilt from the topic; live alerts cannot pause.
incidents.question: How do you repair the scores?

choices.label: Replay from the pre-bug offset into a new table
choices.resultTitle: History fixed, alerts stay live
choices.resultBody: A separate group seeks to the offset at deploy time, rescores 72 hours into a fresh table in about 3 hours, and the live group's 2 s freshness never slips.

choices.label: Reset the live group's offsets to 72 hours ago
choices.resultTitle: Live alerts are now three days late
choices.resultBody: The live scorer must chew through 780M old events before it sees new transactions, so fraud alerts run hours behind during the repair.

choices.label: Ask upstream services to resend 72 hours
choices.resultTitle: Upstream never kept a copy
choices.resultBody: The log is the retained source of truth; producers discarded those events after the ack, so only a fraction comes back and much of it is duplicated.

hints: Retention is 7 days and the bug lasted 3.
Offsets are per consumer group; replay does not have to touch the live one.
Seek a separate group to a timestamp and rebuild beside the live table.

incidents.title: Election-night results fall 3M events behind
incidents.brief: Votecast streams precinct results through 24 partitions to 24 consumer pods on 2 vCPUs each. Election night brings 60k events/s; parsing pins pods at 97% CPU and lag hits 3M.
incidents.constraint: The spike lasts one night, and each precinct's updates must stay in order.
incidents.question: What clears the lag before the networks call the race?

choices.label: Upsize the consumer pods from 2 to 8 vCPUs for tonight
choices.resultTitle: Four times the cores, lag gone in a minute
choices.resultBody: Each pod's worker pool is sized to its cores and keyed by precinct, so 8 vCPUs run four times as many parse workers while each precinct stays in order. CPU falls to 45% and the 3M backlog drains in about a minute. Tomorrow you size back down, paying for one night.

choices.label: Repartition the topic to 96 and quadruple the consumer group
choices.resultTitle: Keys remap mid-count
choices.resultBody: Adding partitions changes which partition each precinct hashes to, so updates already queued on the old partition race new ones on the new partition. 1,400 precinct totals briefly go backwards on air, and the rebalance stalls consumption for 4 minutes.

choices.label: Split parsing into its own stream stage and intermediate topic
choices.resultTitle: A new pipeline that lands next week
choices.resultBody: A separate parse stage is a new service, a new topic and a new deploy path. It cannot be built and tested tonight, so the old pods stay pinned at 97% and lag keeps growing past 5M while the team writes code.

hints: Every partition already has a consumer, and every consumer is CPU-bound.
The load is a one-night spike, not a new normal.
Each pod's worker pool grows with the cores it is given.

incidents.title: Surge pricing stuck at 1.0x in a packed city
incidents.brief: Rides are now keyed by driver_id. The surge job counts ride requests per city inside each consumer, so each sees 1/64 of NYC. Surge shows 1.0x while riders wait 14 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Per-driver ordering must hold, and no partition may turn hot again.
incidents.question: How does surge get a whole-city count without a hot partition?

choices.label: Emit per-city partial counts each second to a city-keyed topic

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Combine locally, then shuffle tiny partial sums; the hot key never touches a partition.

choices.resultTitle: Surge sees the whole city again
choices.resultBody: Each consumer sends one partial count per city per second to a small topic keyed by city_id, and one aggregator sums NYC's 64 partials: 64 messages a second instead of 36k. Surge reads 2.3x and rider wait falls to 4 minutes. Cost: surge trails demand by about 2 s.

choices.label: Key every ride event back by city_id so surge counts locally again
choices.resultTitle: Partition 17 melts again
choices.resultBody: Surge is right for about 20 minutes, then NYC's 36k events/s pile onto one partition again; its consumer pins at 98% CPU and lag climbs past 3M, freezing the driver map.

choices.label: Insert every request in the DB and COUNT per city each second
choices.resultTitle: The pricing store becomes the hot spot
choices.resultBody: 36k inserts/s plus a COUNT over NYC's last five minutes every second push the pricing store to 97% CPU, and surge values arrive 40 s late, too slow to steer drivers.

hints: Surge is a whole-city number, but each consumer only sees a slice of the city.
Counts are additive: partial sums from many places can be combined later.
Aggregate locally first, then send small results to one place per city.

incidents.title: The rebalance storm is back, and worse
incidents.brief: The 15-minute poll limit bought two days. At peak the enrichment API slowed to 2 s a call; 500-record batches take 17 minutes, pods get evicted again and lag hits 20M.
incidents.constraint: Every click must be enriched; the enrichment API scales out fine, each call just takes 2 s at peak.
incidents.question: What keeps every batch far inside the poll limit, however slow calls get?

choices.label: Enrich each batch with 50 calls in flight, not one by one

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Batch time becomes records x latency / concurrency, so slow calls no longer stretch the poll.

choices.resultTitle: Batches finish in 20 seconds
choices.resultBody: With 50 concurrent calls, 500 records take about 20 s even at 2 s per call, far inside the poll limit, so pods stay in the group and the 20M backlog drains in about 40 minutes. Cost: each pod holds 50 open connections to the enrichment API.

choices.label: Raise max.poll.interval.ms once more, from 15 up to 45 minutes
choices.resultTitle: A hung pod now hides for 45 minutes
choices.resultBody: Evictions stop until the API slows further, but a pod that truly hangs now keeps its partitions for 45 minutes before the group notices, and 17-minute batches keep lag near 19M.

nodes.sub: hung pod holding p9 for 45 min

choices.label: Skip enrichment for any record whose call takes over 1 second
choices.resultTitle: Most clicks land without campaign data
choices.resultBody: Batches finish quickly, but at peak 70% of calls take over 1 s, so most clicks reach the warehouse unenriched and every campaign dashboard is wrong for the evening.

hints: Compare the batch time with the poll limit: 500 records at 2 s each.
The API is slow per call, but it happily serves many calls at once.
Batch time is records times latency divided by calls in flight.

incidents.title: The repair job starves live fraud alerts
incidents.brief: The replay group reads 72 hours of transactions at full speed, writing 120k rows/s into the scores database the live scorer shares. DB CPU hits 96%, and live alerts slip from 2 s to 40 s.
incidents.constraint: Live alerts need 2 s freshness, and the repair must finish within 24 hours.
incidents.question: How do you run the repair without hurting live scoring?

choices.label: Cap the replay consumer at 15k events/s with a fetch quota

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Background work gets a fixed share of the shared database and simply runs longer.

choices.resultTitle: Live alerts back to 2 s, repair overnight
choices.resultBody: A consumer quota holds the backfill to 15k events/s, so scores DB CPU falls to 62% and live alerts are fresh within 2 s again. The 780M events now take about 14 hours, finishing overnight and inside the 24-hour deadline.

choices.label: Pause the live scorer entirely until the replay has caught up
choices.resultTitle: Fraud alerts go dark for two hours
choices.resultBody: The replay finishes in about 2 hours with the database to itself, but no live transaction is scored while it runs, so fraud alerts stop during the afternoon peak.

choices.label: Add 30 more replay consumers so the backfill finishes sooner
choices.resultTitle: Writes triple on the same database
choices.resultBody: More replay consumers push writes from 120k to 300k rows/s against the same database. CPU pins at 100%, write timeouts hit the live scorer and its alerts fall 3 minutes behind.

hints: Both consumer groups write to the same database.
The replay's deadline is measured in hours; the live path's in seconds.
Give the backfill a fixed slice of the database and let it take longer.

incidents.title: Delayed mobile events dropped by overly strict watermark
incidents.brief: A Flink billing pipeline with a 5-second bounded-out-of-orderness watermark drops 12% of mobile billing events arriving with cellular network latency.
incidents.constraint: Capture late-arriving financial telemetry without delaying real-time event window emission.
incidents.question: How should late data handling be configured in event-time stream processing?

choices.label: Route late events to a side-output dead-letter stream for reconciliation
choices.resultTitle: Side outputs safely captured late billing events
choices.resultBody: Routing late arrivals to a side-output Kafka topic allows on-time windows to fire while late data is reconciled asynchronously.

choices.label: Increase watermark out-of-orderness delay from 5 seconds to 2 hours
choices.resultTitle: Massive watermark delay broke real-time stream SLAs
choices.resultBody: Holding event-time watermarks back by 2 hours delayed all downstream real-time alerts and bloated operator state memory.

choices.label: Switch pipeline from event time to ingestion processing time clock
choices.resultTitle: Processing time corrupted historical billing calculations
choices.resultBody: Aggregating by processing arrival time lumped delayed events into the wrong calendar days, violating billing accounting rules.

hints: Event time reflects when an action occurred; processing time is when the engine observed it.
Watermarks tell the engine when to close a window and produce a result.
Late data arriving after the watermark can be emitted to a side-output rather than silently dropped.

variants.constraint: The windows feed a nightly invoice run, not a dashboard; nobody reads them for hours. 99.9% of delayed mobile events arrive within 90 minutes.

strm-07-extend-watermark.resultTitle: Late events land in their windows
strm-07-extend-watermark.resultBody: With 2 hours of lateness allowed, 99.9% of delayed events land in their window before it closes, so invoices are complete with no reconciliation job. The cost: 2 hours of extra window state, and results emit later, which the nightly run never notices.

strm-07-side-output.resultBody: Side outputs catch the 12% of late events, but each must be merged back into windows already emitted. That means a second job and invoice corrections, when waiting 2 hours would have fit the nightly run.

hints: Who reads these windows, and how soon?
The results are not needed for hours, and nearly all late events arrive within 90 minutes.
When nobody reads a result for hours, a window can simply stay open longer.

incidents.title: Session window state unbounded growth across idle devices
incidents.brief: A user clickstream session window aggregator accumulates 2TB of RocksDB state because disconnected IoT devices never emit a closing event.
incidents.constraint: Bound state size and prune abandoned sessions without dropping active user streams.
incidents.question: How should state lifecycle and retention be bounded in stream processing?

choices.label: Configure StateTtlConfig with 24-hour expiration on inactive session keys
choices.resultTitle: State TTL purged abandoned sessions automatically
choices.resultBody: Setting an explicit state TTL purges keys that haven't received updates for 24 hours, capping disk state and stabilizing checkpoint times.

choices.label: Purge the entire RocksDB state backend directory every midnight via cron
choices.resultTitle: Blind state purging destroyed active session metrics
choices.resultBody: Deleting backend directories destroyed live session state for actively browsing users, causing inaccurate metric reports.

choices.label: Attach 10TB additional storage disks without modifying state config
choices.resultTitle: Adding disk delayed failure but inflated checkpoint times
choices.resultBody: Unbounded state continued to grow linearly; checkpoint durations climbed past 15 minutes, eventually stalling the cluster.

hints: Session windows group events by periods of activity separated by gaps of inactivity.
Abandoned keys consume storage indefinitely unless explicitly expired.
State TTL allows streaming engines to automatically prune stale state during background compaction.

incidents.title: Consumer group rebalance storm stalls partition consumption
incidents.brief: A single slow consumer thread in a Kafka consumer group exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms`, triggering a group-wide rebalance that pauses all partition processing.
incidents.constraint: Prevent stop-the-world partition rebalances when individual consumer tasks experience lag.
incidents.question: How should consumer assignment and heartbeat configuration be tuned?

choices.label: Adopt CooperativeStickyAssignor and offload long jobs to thread pool
choices.resultTitle: Cooperative rebalancing maintained active stream flow
choices.resultBody: Cooperative rebalancing only revokes partitions that must migrate, allowing unaffected consumers to continue processing without interruption.

choices.label: Increase max.poll.interval.ms to 24 hours to prevent rebalance triggers
choices.resultTitle: Dead consumer instances went undetected for hours
choices.resultBody: Setting a 24-hour poll interval prevented dead workers from being removed, leaving their assigned partitions completely frozen.

choices.label: Consolidate all partition processing into a single monolithic consumer
choices.resultTitle: Single consumer collapsed under total cluster traffic
choices.resultBody: A single consumer instance was completely unable to keep up with 60,000 req/sec, causing consumer lag to grow indefinitely.

hints: Eager rebalancing revokes all partition assignments across the entire group during any membership change.
Cooperative sticky rebalancing migrates only necessary partitions incrementally without stopping the world.
Never perform blocking synchronous I/O directly inside the Kafka poll loop.

incidents.title: Two-phase commit sink transaction timeout aborts checkpoint
incidents.brief: An exactly-once Kafka sink transaction aborts because heavy compaction causes checkpoint duration to exceed `transaction.timeout.ms` (15 minutes).
incidents.constraint: Maintain end-to-end exactly-once delivery semantics without transaction abort churn.
incidents.question: How should transaction coordinator timeouts and checkpoint cadences be coordinated?

choices.label: Align transaction.timeout.ms safely above checkpoint duration limits
choices.resultTitle: Aligned 2PC timeouts eliminated abort cycles
choices.resultBody: Setting Kafka transaction timeout higher than checkpoint duration guarantees open transactions are committed before timing out.

choices.label: Downgrade sink semantic to at-least-once and disable two-phase commit
choices.resultTitle: At-least-once semantics produced duplicate financial transactions
choices.resultBody: Without 2PC transactional guarantees, downstream payment ledgers received duplicate records whenever tasks restarted.

choices.label: Disable streaming checkpoints completely and run purely in memory buffer
choices.resultTitle: Disabling checkpoints caused complete data loss on pod restart
choices.resultBody: Operating without checkpoints eliminates fault tolerance; when a worker died, the entire stream state was permanently lost.

hints: Flink's TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction opens a transaction in Kafka that commits when a checkpoint succeeds.
If checkpointing takes longer than Kafka's transaction timeout, Kafka aborts the open transaction.
Ensure transaction.timeout.ms is safely higher than the checkpoint timeout plus buffer.

variants.constraint: The managed Kafka caps transaction.max.timeout.ms at 15 minutes, and compaction pushes checkpoints to 25. The warehouse upserts every row by a unique txn_id, so duplicates collapse.

strm-10-at-least-once.resultBody: Without two-phase commit nothing waits on a 15-minute transaction, so aborts stop. Replays after a failure rewrite rows the warehouse already has, and the txn_id upsert collapses them: effectively-once end to end, as long as every write keeps that key.

strm-10-align-timeouts.resultTitle: The broker refuses the longer timeout
strm-10-align-timeouts.resultBody: Flink asks for a 30-minute transaction timeout, but the managed broker caps it at 15, so producers fail to start. With 25-minute checkpoints, transactions keep aborting and the sink restarts in a loop.

hints: Can the broker's transaction timeout actually be raised here?
Look at what the warehouse does when it sees the same row twice.
When the sink dedupes by key, the pipeline itself no longer needs transactions.

incidents.title: Key skew hot partition throttles single stream task operator
incidents.brief: A stream analytics pipeline keyed by `merchant_id` routes 40% of all events to a single task slot (Amazon), causing massive backpressure upstream.
incidents.constraint: Distribute workload evenly across all operator parallel tasks without breaking aggregate accuracy.
incidents.question: Which stream repartitioning technique solves extreme key skew?

choices.label: Salt skewed keys with random prefix for pre-aggregation then global merge
choices.resultTitle: Two-stage salted aggregation eliminated key hotspot
choices.resultBody: Adding random salts (e.g. merchant_id_1..10) distributes the hot key across 10 parallel slots before a lightweight final merge.

choices.label: Rebalance every stream event randomly without preserving key grouping
choices.resultTitle: Random rebalance broke stateful per-merchant windowing
choices.resultBody: Scattering events across slots without keys made stateful per-merchant count and sum operations completely inaccurate.

choices.label: Run the hot merchant on a dedicated bare-metal server with 128 cores
choices.resultTitle: Single-core task thread still bottlenecked the key pipeline
choices.resultBody: Because stream tasks are single-threaded per key partition, extra CPU cores sat idle while one core remained 100% pegged.

hints: In stream engines (like Flink keyBy or Kafka partitioning), all events with the same key route to one thread.
When one key accounts for 40% of traffic, vertical scaling fails because a single thread handles the key.
Two-stage aggregation (key + random salt, followed by global sum) parallelizes hot keys seamlessly.
